description: Building data-driven solutions using NASA open datasets, focusing on Earth observation, environmental sustainability and predictive analytics.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a free, open-source web app that answers one question for any place on Earth: is this climate variable really changing, or is it just natural variability? A user picks a place and a variable; the app suggests suitable NASA datasets, plots the monthly series and states in one plain sentence how fast it is changing and whether the change is statistically significant.

Behind that sentence are statistics built for Earth data: the seasonal cycle is removed, the rate is measured with Sen's slope, significance is tested with autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall tests, and false-discovery-rate correction is applied when several variables are tested together.

We demonstrate it on Sapanca Lake, the source of about 70% of Sakarya's drinking water, which reached a record low in January 2026. Of six variables tested together, only air temperature shows a significant trend: +0.52 °C per decade (MERRA-2, adjusted p = 0.002). The claim "rainfall is decreasing" is not supported (GPM IMERG, p = 0.87). A plain regression on the same temperature data misses the warming (p = 0.171).

The tool lets teachers, journalists and local officials test a climate claim before repeating it.
details:
What it does

Earth Trend Detective turns free NASA Earth observation data into a statistically sound answer to four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and is the change statistically significant? It measures and tests; it does not give advice, forecast, or attribute causes.

The app has four screens:

  • Case 1, Sapanca Lake basin: a “suspect board” of six water-cycle and temperature variables tested together.
  • Case 2, the air above Istanbul: surface temperature, temperature at 500 hPa (about 5.5 km) and tropospheric NO2; the 2020 lockdown is marked as a step change, not a trend.
  • Case 3, two regions: the same variable side by side in two places.
  • Explore: three short questions, suggested NASA variables and a live analysis for any coordinates on Earth.

How it works

All numbers come from deterministic Python code; the front end only displays them.

  1. Monthly anomalies: each month minus that calendar month’s long-term mean, so the summer-winter cycle does not hide the long-term change. Months without data stay as gaps on a regular monthly grid, so no month shifts into the wrong season.
  2. Rate of change: Sen’s slope per decade, with a 95% interval from a moving-block bootstrap.
  3. Significance: seasonal Mann-Kendall, autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall (Hamed-Rao) and a t-test on anomalies with an effective-sample-size correction.
  4. Many tests at once: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate across each suspect board, so one variable cannot look significant just by chance.
  5. Not significant yet? A rough estimate of how many years of record would be needed to detect the trend at the current noise level (Weatherhead et al., 1998), because “not significant” does not mean “no change”.
  6. Simple vs corrected: a plain regression on the raw data is shown next to the corrected tests, step by step.

Results (Sapanca, 2000–2026)

  • Air temperature (MERRA-2): +0.52 °C per decade, 95% interval +0.22 to +0.81, FDR-adjusted p = 0.002.
  • Precipitation (GPM IMERG): no significant trend, p = 0.87. NASA POWER, a second NASA product, gives the same answer (p = 0.63).
  • Evapotranspiration, surface runoff, soil moisture (GLDAS) and lake surface temperature (MODIS): no significant trend after correction.
  • Simple vs corrected: a plain regression on raw temperature gives p = 0.171 and misses the warming; after removing the seasonal cycle, the same regression gives p < 0.001.
  • Istanbul: +0.62 °C per decade at the surface (MERRA-2) and +0.38 °C per decade at 500 hPa (AIRS), both p < 0.001.

Benefits and intended impact

Free NASA data exists, but testing a claim such as “the lake is shrinking because rainfall is decreasing” correctly requires expertise. Wrong answers are costly in both directions: unnecessary alarm, or being caught unprepared. Our users are people who need to check a climate claim before repeating it: a geography teacher in class, municipal staff writing a report, a local journalist. The tool works anywhere on Earth, the data is free and the code is open source. Our goal is that every student can become the data detective of their own region.

Tools and languages

  • Python: FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with Alpine.js, Plotly.js and Lucide icons (no build step).
  • NASA access tools: Giovanni (area-averaged time series), AppEEARS (MODIS point samples), NASA POWER API (live data).
  • Hosting: Render (Docker).
  • Version control: GitHub. 16 automated tests (pytest).

What makes it creative

  • The question is framed as a detective case: variables are “suspects” questioned together, and the verdict is corrected for multiple testing.
  • It shows why the method matters: on the same data, the simple approach misses a 0.5 °C-per-decade warming that the corrected tests detect.
  • It reports honestly when the answer is “not detectable yet” and estimates how much longer a record would be needed.

Factors we considered

  • Sapanca Lake level is also driven by water management; the tool measures the climate side only and does not explain the lake level.
  • Grid cells are large (about 25 km for GLDAS, about 50 km for MERRA-2 and POWER, about 100 km for AIRS): results describe a basin and its surroundings, not a district.
  • We cross-check key results with a second NASA product. When two products disagree on a trend, we do not report that trend.
  • No AI model runs inside the app, every number is computed by code and every explanation sentence comes from a fixed template.
